TEST_DEFECT_not_a_policy_defect.cause: my matrix omitted the s3:prefix context entry, so the Allow's StringLike condition could not match
TEST_DEFECT_not_a_policy_defect.conclusion: the POLICY is correct for listing. The matrix cell was wrong, not the deployment. Recorded as a test defect rather than silently re-scored.

WHAT_FAILED.my_error: I used six INDEPENDENT Allow statements, which is correct, but a SINGLE shared condition list in the corresponding Deny.
WHAT_FAILED.root_cause: DenyValidation2AtAnyUnregisteredVersion uses ONE shared condition StringNotEquals s3:versionid = [all six VersionIds]. When key A is probed with key B's REGISTERED VersionId, that value IS in the shared list, so StringNotEquals is FALSE and the deny does not fire. No Allow matches either, because each Allow pins its own key to its own version — so the request falls through to IMPLICIT deny.
WHAT_FAILED.security_effect: NONE — access is still REFUSED in every failing cell. There is NO over-permission: no cross-key or unregistered-version read is possible.
WHAT_FAILED.why_it_is_still_a_failure: the registration required EXPLICIT deny. An implicit deny is a weaker guarantee: it can be overridden by any future Allow elsewhere in the policy space, whereas an explicit deny cannot. The owner's requirement to 'mechanically demonstrate that every statement independently binds its own VersionId' is exactly what this construction fails to do at the DENY layer — the six-key/one-condition error the owner warned about, caught by the test designed to catch it.
